notes:
I've written notes for all 24 verses, but some parts of your request have gaps. My search budget ran out before I could reach several sources, so there is nothing below from Lutheran, Pentecostal, Orthodox, prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teachers, and no pages from bibleodyssey.org, newadvent on the skin garments, or oca.org. The NET Bible page came back with the wrong chapter. The only NET note I have is the one Precept Austin quotes at v. 1. Some verses (2, 12, 13, 17–20, 23) only have one or two notes.

**v. 1**
- Allen Ross points to a Hebrew wordplay linking 3:1 to 2:25: Adam and Eve were "naked" (arom); and the serpent was more crafty (arum, "shrewd"). Their nakedness meant they knew nothing of evil. https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis-3-commentary
- Modern scholarship (NET note, as quoted by Precept Austin): the serpent's craftiness is aimed at the couple's integrity. At the start they are naked and he is shrewd; afterwards they will be clothed and he will be cursed. https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis-3-commentary
- Guzik admits that the text here does not, by itself alone, clearly identify the serpent as Satan, but says the rest of the Bible makes this clear (Rev 12:9; 20:2). He holds that the creature became a snake only under the curse. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-3/
- Most authorities cited on Precept Austin hold that Satan was using, or "possessing," a real serpent. https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis-3-commentary
- Jamieson, Fausset & Brown: a real serpent was the tool of a higher agent, Satan. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Gen/Gen_003.cfm
- Wesley (Methodist) is more cautious. He says it is not certain whether it was only the appearance of a serpent or a real one possessed by the devil. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/genesis/3.htm
- The serpent's question: he twists God's generous permission into a purely negative rule, "God won't let you eat of every tree." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-3/ Another note on Precept Austin says Satan wanted Eve to see God as stingy and restrictive. https://temp.preceptaustin.org/index.php/genesis-3-commentary

**vv. 2–3**
- Eve leaves out God's words "any" and "freely," which seems to play down her freedom. https://temp.preceptaustin.org/index.php/genesis-3-commentary
- She adds "or touch it." Guzik says avoiding the tree was wise, but presenting human rules as God's commands is dangerous. He also blames Adam for passing on God's word poorly. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-3/
- MacArthur, citing Leupold, argues the real fall happened before the eating: once Eve stopped fully trusting God's goodness, she had already fallen. https://www.gty.org/sermons/90-238/the-fall-of-man-part-1

**v. 4**
- The serpent's "You will not surely die" directly contradicts God's "You shall surely die" in 2:17. https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis-3-commentary
- Guzik sums up the lie as "sin is not bad, and God is not good." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-3/
- Wesley sees a pattern Satan still uses: he questions whether something is a sin, denies any danger, then promises a benefit. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/genesis/3.htm

**v. 5**
- Guzik: the temptation worked because it held some truth. Their eyes were opened, but only to their own sin. "Like God" is the very ambition that brought Satan down. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-3/
- Wesley: the serpent twisted the tree's name. It was meant to teach the practical knowledge of duty and disobedience, and Satan made it sound like abstract, godlike knowledge. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/genesis/3.htm

**v. 6**
- Guzik matches the three appeals to 1 John 2:16 (lust of the flesh, lust of the eyes, pride of life) and to Jesus' three temptations. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-3/
- **Where traditions differ: was Adam there?**
 - Guzik and other Precept Austin writers place Adam beside her, passive. Lowell Johnson says he watched, saw she did not die, then ate with his eyes open. https://www.preceptaustin.org/sermons-genesis-lowell-johnson
 - Wesley thinks it likely he was not with her when she was tempted. He believes Adam came afterwards and she persuaded him. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/genesis-3.html
- **Adam as head of the race:** Guzik holds that Adam, not Eve, bears responsibility for the fall and for death (Rom 5:12). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-3/ Wesley says Adam knew he stood as a public person, so his disobedience would be fatal to all his descendants. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/genesis-3.html

**v. 7**
- Guzik quotes Barnhouse's guess that they may have been clothed in light before the fall. He adds that after the fall everything looked worse. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-3/
- Wesley: they cared more about saving face before each other than about getting God's pardon. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/genesis-3.html
- Precept Austin calls the idea that the sin was sexual "dubious." It notes that 3:5 and 3:22 treat knowing good and evil as something belonging to God. https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis-3-commentary

**v. 8**
- Wesley: God came walking slowly, "as one slow to anger," in the cool of the day, and gave warning that He was coming. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/genesis-3.html
- Guzik: hiding shows they knew their fig-leaf covering had failed. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-3/

**v. 9**
- Guzik lists the purposes of "Where are you?": to make Adam feel lost, to lead him to confess, to show God's sorrow, and to show that God seeks the lost. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-3/
- Wesley calls the question a gracious pursuit in order to his recovery. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/genesis/3.htm
- God questions Adam first, which these writers take as a sign that He held Adam responsible as head of the family. https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis-3-commentary

**vv. 10–11**
- God already knew. He asked so that Adam would confess; the passage shows how reluctant sinners are to admit their sin. https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis-3-commentary
- Wesley: God wants confession "not that he may be informed, but that we may be humbled." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/genesis/3.htm

**vv. 12–13**
- Clarke: Adam admits what he did but shifts the blame onto God and the woman. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/genesis-3.html
- Wesley: neither fully owns the fault. Adam blames his wife and quietly blames God; Eve blames the serpent. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/genesis-3.html

**v. 14**
- Wesley: God did not question the serpent, because it was already convicted and would never be forgiven. "Dust" stands for a low, despised condition. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/genesis/3.htm
- Scofield (on Precept Austin): crawling is the result of the curse, and the creature may have been beautiful before. https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis-3-commentary

**v. 15** (the "first gospel")
- Protestant traditional reading:
 - MacArthur: the woman's seed is Christ, and the serpent's seed is Satan and unbelievers. https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis-3-commentary
 - Matthew Henry: Here was the dawning of the gospel day. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Gen/Gen_003.cfm
 - Wesley sees Christ's incarnation, suffering (the bruised heel) and victory in the verse. He says by faith in this promise, our first parents, and the patriarchs before the flood, were justified and saved. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/genesis-3.html
 - Clarke reads "seed of the woman" as pointing to the virgin birth. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/amp/genesis/3-15.html
- Catholic reading:
 - The Douay-Rheims has "she shall crush." catholic.com says modern translations follow the Hebrew "he," and the "she" reading probably began as a copyist's error. It says the idea is still true, because Mary crushed the serpent indirectly, through her Son. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/print-edition/who-will-crush-the-serpents-head
 - A second catholic.com article says the Hebrew gender is ambiguous and the Septuagint made it masculine. It lists several meanings that can all be true together, including Mary's conflict with the devil. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/print-edition/the-woman-the-seed-the-serpent
 - The Catholic Encyclopedia disagrees with the copyist-error view. It calls "she" an "explanatory version," not a corruption, and calls this verse the first prophecy of Mary. https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/15464b.htm
 - Another catholic.com answer reads the seed broadly as the Church, and Mary as the "New Eve." https://www.catholic.com/qa/genesis-315-who-crushes-the-serpents-head

**v. 16**
- Ellicott: the woman is not cursed as the serpent was, but punished as next in guilt. https://biblehub.com/genesis/3-16.htm
- **Where traditions differ: "your desire"**
 - Calvin (Reformed): her desires become subject to her husband's will. Wendy Alsup says Wesley held a similar view. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/article/problems-with-a-new-reading-of-an-old-verse/
 - Susan Foh (1975) argued the desire is to control him, based on 4:7. This is now the common complementarian view, defended at TGC by Claire Smith. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/article/a-sidebar-named-desire/
 - Guzik takes the same view. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-3/
 - Alsup argues for an older reading: an idolatrous longing for what only God can give. She says the control idea is read into the text. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/article/problems-with-a-new-reading-of-an-old-verse/
 - Constable lists four views, adding a continued sexual desire despite painful childbirth. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/3-16.html
- **Is "he will rule" a command or a description?**
 - Matthew Henry reads it as God's command "Wives, be subject." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/3-16.htm
 - GotQuestions says it is not a biblical command for men to dominate women. https://www.gotquestions.org/desire-husband-rule.html

**vv. 17–19**
- Work itself is not the punishment, since Adam worked before the fall (2:15). The penalty is sweat, toil and the resistance of nature. https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis-3-commentary
- Guzik links the thorns to Jesus' crown of thorns. He says "dust you shall return" promises an end to toil, but through death, not rescue. https://es.enduringword.com/comentario-biblico/genesis-03/
- JFB: man became mortal. His body began to change toward death even though he did not die that day. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Gen/Gen_003.cfm

**v. 20**
- Barnes: naming her "Eve" shows Adam believed salvation would somehow come through the woman. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/3-16.html
- Wesley hints at the same, calling it an instance of Adam's faith in the word of God. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-first-book-of-moses-called-genesis/

**v. 21**
- Wesley: the first thing that died was a sacrifice, or Christ in a figure. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-first-book-of-moses-called-genesis/
- Precept Austin: the fig leaves show that human efforts fall short. An animal died instead of Adam and Eve, a picture of God giving His Son. https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis-3-commentary

**v. 22**
- Henry Morris reads "one of Us" as a glimpse into the councils of the triune God, matching Genesis 1:26. https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis-3-commentary
- Clarke quotes a paraphrase taking it as "the man who *was* like one of us" but is now fallen. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/genesis-3.html
- Wesley's note on 3:5 offers a related point: they gained knowledge of good and evil as an experience of misery, not as gods do. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/genesis/3.htm

**vv. 23–24**
- Matthew Henry and Wesley: man was sent to a place of toil, not to a place of torment. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Gen/Gen_003.cfm
- Wesley: being driven out stands for losing the fellowship with God that made paradise. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-first-book-of-moses-called-genesis/
- Guzik: cherubim are always linked with God's presence and glory. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-3/
- Clarke: Adam was unwilling to leave, so God "drove" him out. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/genesis-3.html
